title: Equality of opportunity in public employment
plain: All citizens get equal opportunity in jobs and appointments under the State. No citizen can be made ineligible or discriminated against for a government job only because of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. The State may still reserve posts for backward classes and SC/ST that are not adequately represented.
quote: (1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.
notes: Constitution of India, Legislative Department edition as on 1 May 2024. Clauses (3)-(6) (residence requirements, reservation, promotion with consequential seniority) summarised, not quoted.

title: Abolition of titles
plain: The State cannot confer titles, except military or academic distinctions, and Indian citizens cannot accept titles from a foreign State.
quote: (1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. (2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State.
notes: Clauses (3)-(4) restrict non-citizens and office holders accepting foreign titles or presents without the President's consent.

title: Reasonable restrictions on free speech
plain: Freedom of speech and expression is not absolute. The State can make laws imposing reasonable restrictions on it in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
quote: (2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
notes: Clauses (3)-(6) allow reasonable restrictions on the other Article 19 freedoms (assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) on their own listed grounds.

title: Protection in respect of conviction
plain: No one can be convicted under a law that did not exist when the act was done, or given a heavier penalty than the law then allowed; no one can be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence; and no accused person can be forced to be a witness against themselves.
quote: (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. (2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
notes: Constitution of India, Legislative Department edition as on 1 May 2024.

title: No child labour in factories, mines or hazardous work
plain: No child below fourteen may be employed in a factory or mine or in any other hazardous employment.
quote: No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.
notes: Constitution of India, Legislative Department edition as on 1 May 2024.

title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
plain: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination can set up and run religious and charitable institutions, manage its own religious affairs, and own, acquire and administer property in accordance with law.
quote: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right— (a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; (b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and (d) to administer such property in accordance with law.
notes: Articles 27 and 28 (no taxes to promote a religion; religious instruction in educational institutions) are in the same Part but not entered.

title: Protection of interests of minorities
plain: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it, and no citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or State-aided educational institution only on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.
quote: (1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. (2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
notes: Constitution of India, Legislative Department edition as on 1 May 2024.

title: Minorities' educational institutions
plain: All minorities, whether based on religion or language, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
quote: (1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
notes: Clause (1A) protects such institutions' property on compulsory acquisition; clause (2) bars the State from discriminating against them in giving aid.

title: High Courts' power to issue writs
plain: Every High Court can issue directions, orders or writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) to any person or authority, including the Government, within its territory, to enforce fundamental rights and for any other purpose. It is often the first court approached when a fundamental right is violated.
quote: (1) Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
notes: Part VI of the Constitution. Clause (2) lets a High Court act where the cause of action arises wholly or partly in its territory.

title: Theft and its punishment
plain: Theft is dishonestly moving someone's movable property out of their possession without consent, intending to take it. Punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years, or a fine, or both. On a second or later conviction: rigorous imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine. If the stolen property is worth less than ₹5,000, it is the person's first conviction and the property or its value is returned, the punishment is community service.
quote: (2) Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both and in case of second or subsequent conviction of any person under this section, he shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years and with fine: Provided that in cases of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and a person is convicted for the first time, shall upon return of the value of property or restoration of the stolen property, shall be punished with community service.
notes: Gazette of India Extraordinary No. 53, 25 Dec 2023 (Act 45 of 2023), in force from 1 Jul 2024. s.303(1) defines theft. Aggravated forms (snatching s.304, theft in a dwelling and others) have separate sections not entered here. Replaces IPC ss.378-379 for offences on or after 1 Jul 2024.

title: When police may arrest without a warrant
plain: Police can arrest without a warrant or a Magistrate's order only in listed situations, e.g. a cognizable offence committed in front of them; a credible complaint or reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence punishable with up to 7 years, but only if the officer believes the person did it and arrest is necessary (to prevent further offences, for proper investigation, to stop evidence tampering or witness threats, or to secure court attendance), with reasons recorded in writing; credible information of an offence punishable with more than 7 years or death; proclaimed offenders; possession of suspected stolen property; obstructing police or escaping custody. Where arrest is not needed in an up-to-7-years case, the officer must record reasons for not arresting.
quote: 35. (1) Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person— (a) who commits, in the presence of a police officer, a cognizable offence; or (b) against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years whether with or without fine, if the following conditions are satisfied ... and the police officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing
notes: Gazette of India Extraordinary No. 54, 25 Dec 2023 (Act 46 of 2023), in force from 1 Jul 2024. Further sub-sections of s.35 (notice of appearance instead of arrest, and other limits) were not read for this entry. Replaces CrPC s.41.

title: Right to know the grounds of arrest and of bail
plain: A person arrested without a warrant must be told at once the full particulars of the offence or other grounds for the arrest. If the offence is bailable, the police must tell them they are entitled to be released on bail and can arrange sureties.
quote: 47. (1) Every police officer or other person arresting any person without warrant shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest. (2) Where a police officer arrests without warrant any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence, he shall inform the person arrested that he is entitled to be released on bail and that he may arrange for sureties on his behalf.
notes: Replaces CrPC s.50.

title: Family or friend must be told of the arrest
plain: The police must at once inform a relative, friend or other person nominated by the arrested person (and the designated police officer in the district) about the arrest and where the person is being held, and must tell the arrested person of this right when they reach the police station.
quote: 48. (1) Every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Sanhita shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his relatives, friends or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information and also to the designated police officer in the district.
notes: Replaces CrPC s.50A.

title: 24-hour limit on police custody without a Magistrate
plain: Police cannot keep a person arrested without a warrant for longer than is reasonable, and never more than 24 hours (excluding travel time to the Magistrate) without a special order of a Magistrate.
quote: 58. No police officer shall detain in custody a person arrested without warrant for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable, and such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 187, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court, whether having jurisdiction or not.
notes: Replaces CrPC s.57. Mirrors Article 22(2) of the Constitution.

title: Consumer rights
plain: The Act lists six consumer rights: protection against hazardous goods and services; to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price; access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices; to be heard at appropriate forums; to seek redressal against unfair or restrictive trade practices and exploitation; and consumer awareness.
quote: (9) "consumer rights" includes,— (i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property; (ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices; (iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora; (v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (vi) the right to consumer awareness;
notes: Gazette text of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019) hosted by the Department of Consumer Affairs.

title: Conditions before retrenching a worker
plain: A worker with at least one year of continuous service cannot be retrenched until (a) they get one month's written notice with reasons, or one month's wages instead of notice; (b) they are paid compensation of 15 days' average pay for every completed year of service (or part over six months); and (c) notice is served on the Government authority as prescribed.
quote: 70. No worker employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until— (a) the worker has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the worker has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the notice; (b) the worker has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' average pay, or average pay of such days as may be notified by the appropriate Government, for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months; and (c) notice in such manner as may be prescribed is served on the appropriate Government or such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification.
notes: Gazette of India Extraordinary, 29 Sep 2020 (Act 35 of 2020); the Labour Codes came into force on 21 Nov 2025 (FACT-LABOUR-CODES-COMMENCEMENT). Applies to 'workers' as defined in s.2(zr) (managers, administrators and supervisors earning above the notified limit are excluded). Larger establishments need prior Government permission for retrenchment under a separate chapter, not entered here. Replaces Industrial Disputes Act s.25F.

title: What counts as retrenchment
plain: Retrenchment means the employer ending a worker's service for any reason other than disciplinary punishment. It does not include voluntary retirement, retirement at superannuation age, non-renewal or contractual termination of a fixed contract, end of fixed-term employment, or termination for continued ill-health.
quote: (zh) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a worker for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include— (i) voluntary retirement of the worker; or (ii) retirement of the worker on reaching the age of superannuation; or (iii) termination of the service of the worker as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment between the employer and the worker concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or (iv) termination of service of the worker as a result of completion of tenure of fixed term employment; or (v) termination of the service of a worker on the ground of continued ill-health;
notes: Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s.2(zh).

title: Who is a 'worker'
plain: A 'worker' is anyone employed in an industry for manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for pay. It excludes people employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity, supervisors earning more than ₹18,000 a month (or a limit the Central Government notifies), apprentices, and members of the armed forces, police or prison staff.
quote: (zr) "worker" means any person (except an apprentice as defined under clause (aa) of section 2 of the Apprentices Act, 1961) employed in any industry to do any manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward ... but does not include any such person— ... (iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or (iv) who is employed in a supervisory capacity drawing wages exceeding eighteen thousand rupees per month or an amount as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time
notes: Whether a notified amount has replaced ₹18,000 was not checked. Managers and senior staff outside 'worker' depend on their employment contract (Indian Contract Act s.73 for breach).

title: Grounds for divorce
plain: Either spouse can ask the court for divorce on grounds including: adultery; cruelty; desertion for at least two continuous years before the petition; conversion to another religion; incurable unsound mind or serious mental disorder; venereal disease in a communicable form; renouncing the world by entering a religious order; or not being heard of as alive for seven years. The Act also gives the wife certain additional grounds.
quote: 13. Divorce.—(1) Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, may, on a petition presented by either the husband or the wife, be dissolved by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other party— (i) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, had voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than his or her spouse; or (ia) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, treated the petitioner with cruelty; or (ib) has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition; or (ii) has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion; ...
notes: Consolidated text with amendment footnotes, hosted by the Punjab & Haryana High Court (same host as the library's CPC source); India Code timed out (504) on 7 Nov 2026. Applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs (s.2). Section 13(1A) (no cohabitation for a year after a decree of judicial separation or restitution) and 13(2) (wife's additional grounds) exist but were not quoted. Other religions and civil marriages are governed by other Acts not in this library.

title: Divorce by mutual consent
plain: Both spouses can jointly file for divorce in the district court if they have lived separately for one year or more, cannot live together and have agreed the marriage should end. They make a second joint motion no earlier than six months and no later than eighteen months after filing; if the petition has not been withdrawn, the court, after hearing them and being satisfied, grants the divorce.
quote: 13B. Divorce by mutual consent.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce may be presented to the district court by both the parties to a marriage together, whether such marriage was solemnized before or after the commencement of the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (68 of 1976), on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved. (2) On the motion of both the parties made not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition referred to in sub-section (1) and not later than eighteen months after the said date, if the petition is not withdrawn in the meantime, the court shall, on being satisfied, after hearing the parties and after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, that a marriage has been solemnized and that the averments in the petition are true, pass a decree of divorce declaring the marriage to be dissolved
notes: Inserted by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976. Courts have interpreted the six-month period; no judgments are in this library, so none are cited.

title: No divorce petition within one year of marriage
plain: A divorce petition generally cannot be filed until one year has passed since the marriage. The court may allow it earlier only in a case of exceptional hardship to the petitioner or exceptional depravity of the other spouse.
quote: 14. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, it shall not be competent for any court to entertain any petition for dissolution of a marriage by a decree of divorce, unless at the date of the presentation of the petition one year has elapsed since the date of the marriage: Provided that the court may, upon application made to it in accordance with such rules as may be made by the High Court in that behalf, allow a petition to be presented before one year has elapsed since the date of the marriage on the ground that the case is one of exceptional hardship to the petitioner or of exceptional depravity on the part of the respondent
notes: Proviso checked in full against the PDF text; it continues that leave obtained by misrepresentation or concealment can affect the decree.
